corpus_definition: Very small in degree or amount.

forms.definition: a rude action that shows you do not respect someone
forms.example: She took his silence as a personal slight.
forms.note: Belongs to slight = to insult or ignore someone, not 'very small in amount'.

forms.definition: to insult someone by ignoring them or treating them as unimportant
forms.example: He felt slighted when nobody asked for his opinion.
forms.note: Belongs to slight = to insult or ignore someone, not 'very small in amount'. Formal.

forms.definition: very small in size, amount or importance
forms.example: I have a slight headache, but I can still go to class.

syn.note: Easy, general word; slight is often used for changes, problems and differences.
Small and not very important: a minor problem.
Easy word, but it usually comes before the noun: a little problem.
Even smaller than slight, and often about size, not degree.

ant.note: Large or important: a major change.
Quite large in amount or degree; a bit formal.
Easy, everyday opposite.

forms.definition: a little; not very much
forms.example: The bus was slightly late this morning.

syn.note: Easy and very close in meaning.
Same meaning, more informal.
Same idea, more formal.

ant.note: By a large amount.
Very much; a bit formal.

context.text: There was a slight change in the timetable today. Our lesson started slightly later, at ten instead of nine.

reviewer_note: The noun and verb slight (= insult) are a different meaning, shown as other_meaning; 'not in the slightest' is just the superlative.

corpus_definition: To break something into many small pieces with force.

forms.definition: the loud sound or act of something breaking into pieces
forms.example: We heard the smash of a plate in the kitchen.
forms.note: In informal English, a smash (or smash hit) is also a very successful song or film.

syn.note: A loud noise of something hitting or breaking.
A sudden loud noise, not always of breaking.

forms.definition: to break something into many pieces by hitting or dropping it hard
forms.example: The ball smashed the kitchen window.

syn.note: Easy, general word; smash means breaking with a lot of force and noise.
To break suddenly into very small pieces, often about glass.
To press something hard so it breaks or loses its shape.
To damage something so badly that it cannot be used.

ant.note: To make something broken work or look good again.
Easy, everyday word for repair.

forms.definition: broken into many pieces
forms.example: Be careful, there is smashed glass on the floor.
forms.note: In informal British English, smashed can also mean very drunk.

syn.note: Easy, general word.
Broken into very small pieces, often about glass.

ant.note: In one piece, not broken.

forms.definition: very good or enjoyable
forms.example: We had a smashing time at the party.
forms.note: Belongs to smash = great success; old-fashioned informal British English, not breaking things.
There is no adverb made from smash.

context.text: A football smashed our neighbour's window yesterday. My little brother helped to clean up the smashed glass, and then he paid for a new window from his pocket money.

reviewer_note: smashing (= great) is a separate informal meaning, shown as other_meaning; smasher left out as rare.

corpus_definition: To make a short, sharp sound.

forms.definition: a short, sharp sound, like something breaking or closing
forms.example: I heard a loud snap when the branch broke.
forms.note: Informally, a snap is also a photo: 'holiday snaps'.

syn.note: A sudden sharp sound, like wood or a whip.
A short quiet sound, like a switch or a pen.
A short sound like a balloon breaking.

forms.definition: to break suddenly with a short, sharp sound
forms.example: The dry branch snapped under his foot.
forms.note: Also: snap your fingers (make a sound with your fingers). In other meanings, snap means to speak angrily or to take a quick photo.

syn.note: To break with a sharp sound.
Easy, general word; it does not say anything about the sound.
To make a short quiet sound.

forms.definition: made or done very quickly, without planning
forms.example: He made a snap decision to leave.
forms.note: Belongs to snap = do something suddenly; used only before a noun: a snap decision, a snap election.

forms.definition: short, clever and quick; also speaking in an annoyed way
forms.example: The advert has a snappy title.
forms.note: Belongs to snap = quick or angry speech, not a sharp sound. Informal.

forms.definition: in a quick, clever or annoyed way
forms.example: She answered snappily because she was tired.
forms.note: Goes with snappy (quick or annoyed), not the sound meaning. Not very common.

context.text: We walked through the forest near Chimgan, and dry sticks snapped under our feet. Every snap made the birds fly away.

reviewer_note: Many meanings (sound, break, speak angrily, photo); map anchored to the sound/break meaning. snapshot left out as a compound.

corpus_definition: To take something away quickly and suddenly.

forms.definition: a quick movement of the hand to take something
forms.example: He made a snatch at the keys but missed.

syn.note: Same idea, more common: make a grab for something.

forms.definition: a short part of a conversation or a song
forms.example: I heard snatches of their conversation through the wall.
forms.note: Belongs to snatch = a small piece you hear, not taking something quickly.

forms.definition: to take something quickly and suddenly from someone or something
forms.example: A man snatched her bag and ran away.

syn.note: Very close and more common in everyday English.
To take something quickly and firmly; more formal.
Easy, general word; it does not say how fast.
Snatching is often a kind of stealing, but you can also snatch your own things.

ant.note: To return something to the person who had it.

forms.note: There is no adjective made from snatch.
There is no adverb made from snatch.

people.definition: a person who takes things from people quickly and runs away
people.example: Police caught the bag snatcher near the bazaar.

context.text: At the park, a big bird snatched a piece of bread from my sister's hand. She tried to get it back, but the bird made another snatch and flew away.

reviewer_note: Noun snatch has two meanings: the quick grab (existing) and a short piece of conversation/music (other_meaning).

corpus_definition: To move somewhere quietly so that no one sees you.

forms.definition: the quality of doing things secretly and not honestly
forms.example: His sneakiness made the other players angry.

syn.note: Keeping things secret, not always in a dishonest way.
Not telling the truth or not being fair.

ant.note: Being open and telling the truth.

forms.definition: to go somewhere quietly and secretly so that nobody notices you
forms.example: The kids sneaked into the kitchen to eat the cake.
forms.note: Past tense: sneaked (British) or snuck (American, informal).

syn.note: To move slowly and quietly so people don't hear you.
To go somewhere quickly and quietly: slip out of the room.
To walk on your toes so you make no noise.

forms.definition: doing things in a secret and slightly dishonest way
forms.example: That was a sneaky way to win the game.

syn.note: Clever at tricking people in a secret way.
Not telling the truth; stronger and more general.
Hidden from others, not always in a bad way.

ant.note: Open and telling the truth.
Not hiding anything.

forms.definition: done secretly or without warning
forms.example: The shop gave us a sneak preview of the new phone.
forms.note: Only before a noun: a sneak preview, a sneak attack.

forms.definition: felt but not said, often without a good reason
forms.example: I have a sneaking feeling that he forgot my birthday.
forms.note: Belongs to sneak = a feeling you keep secret: a sneaking suspicion, not moving quietly.

forms.definition: in a secret and slightly dishonest way
forms.example: He sneakily took the last piece of bread.

syn.note: Without others knowing, not always in a bad way.
In a clever, secret and tricky way.

ant.note: Without hiding anything.
In a true and fair way.

people.definition: a soft sports shoe with a rubber bottom
people.example: I bought new sneakers for the gym.
people.note: American English; British people say trainers. The name came from moving quietly in soft shoes, but today it just means sports shoes.

context.text: After dinner, my little brother tried to sneak out to play football. It was a sneaky plan, but Mum saw him at the door.

reviewer_note: Noun sneak (= a person who tells on others) is old-fashioned British and left out; sneaker shown as other_meaning thing.

corpus_definition: to stay in water for a long time to get very wet

forms.definition: a time when you leave something in water, or take a long bath
forms.example: Give the beans a good soak before you cook them.

syn.note: For people: a long bath is sometimes called a soak.

forms.definition: to leave something in water, or stay in water, for a long time
forms.example: Let the dirty plates soak in hot water for an hour.

syn.note: Mostly for tea, herbs or food in liquid.
Easy, general word; soak means very wet for a long time.
To make someone or something completely wet, often by rain.
To put something in liquid for a very short time.

ant.note: To take the water out of something.

forms.definition: completely wet
forms.example: We got soaked in the rain on the way home.

syn.note: Easy word; soaked is much stronger.
Very close: completely wet.

ant.note: With no water on or in it.

forms.definition: very wet; often used as 'soaking wet'
forms.example: Your coat is soaking wet!

forms.note: There is no adverb made from soak; people say 'soaking wet'.

context.text: It rained all day in Tashkent and I came home soaked. My mum told me to soak my feet in warm water so I wouldn't get a cold.

reviewer_note: Corpus definition uses the intransitive meaning; the transitive 'leave something in water' is the same meaning and covered in the verb definition.

corpus_definition: Programs used by a computer to function.

forms.definition: the programs that a computer or phone uses to work
forms.example: You need to update the software on your phone.
forms.note: Uncountable: say 'a piece of software' or 'a program', not 'a software'.

syn.note: One single piece of software. British spelling for computers is also program.
A program, especially one on a phone.
Formal word for app or program.

ant.note: Hardware is the machine you can touch; software is the programs inside it.

forms.note: There is no verb made from software.
There is no adjective made from software; use it before a noun: a software company.

context.text: My cousin works for a software company in Tashkent. She writes software for banks and online shops.

reviewer_note: Software is itself a compound (soft + ware); no family forms. software developer/engineer are compounds, left out.

corpus_definition: Relating to the light or heat from the sun.

forms.note: Sun has the same meaning area but is an old English word, not made from solar. Solarium is rare.
There is no common verb made from solar.

forms.definition: connected with the sun or using its light and heat
forms.example: They put solar panels on the roof of the school.
forms.note: Used only before a noun: solar energy, solar power, a solar panel.

syn.note: Lunar is about the moon; solar is about the sun: a lunar eclipse, a solar eclipse.

context.text: Uzbekistan has a lot of sunny days, so solar energy is a good idea here. Many new houses now have solar panels.

reviewer_note: Adjective only, used before nouns; sun listed as not_family. solar system is its own phrase entry.

corpus_definition: The sun and all the objects that travel around it.
usage_note: Usually with the or our: 'the solar system', 'our solar system'. Can also mean any star with planets around it: 'another solar system'.

relations.note: Scientific phrase for any star with planets; solar system is the common word.
Much bigger: a galaxy has billions of stars, and our solar system is a tiny part of one.
Everything that exists in space; much bigger than the solar system.

context.text: There are eight planets in our solar system. Jupiter is the biggest planet in the solar system, and Earth is the third from the sun.

reviewer_note: Corpus example says 'Nine planets' (out of date since 2006; now eight). Context uses eight; reviewer may want to fix the corpus example.

corpus_definition: Being the only one of its kind.

forms.note: The noun sole (bottom of your foot or shoe; also a fish) is a different word with the same spelling, not made from this sole.
There is no verb from this meaning of sole.

forms.definition: being the only one; not shared with anyone else
forms.example: He is the sole owner of this small shop.
forms.note: Used only before a noun: the sole survivor, the sole reason.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with the same meaning.
Just one: a single reason.
Only for one person or group: exclusive rights.

ant.note: Shared by two or more people: joint owners.
Used or owned by more than one person.

forms.definition: only; not involving anyone or anything else
forms.example: The decision was made solely by the director.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with the same meaning.
Informal and very common.
Formal: only for one thing or person.
Completely; often used together: entirely and solely.

ant.note: Only in some way, not completely.

context.text: Aziz is the sole owner of a small bakery in Samarkand. He is solely responsible for buying flour, baking and selling the bread.

reviewer_note: Homonym trap: sole (foot/shoe, fish) is a different word, so the noun slot is no_form with a note, not other_meaning.
